definition: Storage facilities are repurposed geological formations that hold natural gas between the pipeline system and the end user, acting as a buffer that absorbs the mismatch between continuous pipeline flow and cyclical burner-tip demand; gas held in storage must be at higher pressure than the pipeline to allow outflow back into it.
core_idea: Pipelines must run continuously but gas demand does not, so gas that isn't needed immediately after transport has to be either stored or flared off; storage absorbs this mismatch, smooths the two annual demand peaks (winter heating, summer air-conditioning load on power generation), and provides a safety margin against short-term regional demand swings.
key_points: Storage prevents having to burn off or waste excess gas when there's no immediate consumer demand.
Pipelines must run continuously, but demand does not, so gas has to be either stored or flared off.
Storage must be held at higher pressure than the pipeline to allow outflow back into it.
Demand peaks twice a year: winter (heating) and summer (air conditioning load on power generation).
Storage also provides a safety margin against short-term, regional swings in demand.
Gas that isn't needed immediately after transport can be stored for very long periods (much of the gas produced is already geologically ancient).

Storage sites are located at both ends of pipelines: gas commonly passes through a first set of storage facilities near producing regions (e.g., the U.S. Gulf Coast near refineries and pipeline hubs) and a second set near the consuming region before final delivery.

Facilities differ mainly along two dimensions: how much gas they can hold and how fast it can be withdrawn; construction cost, storage quantity, and injection/withdrawal speed depend on local geology.
Facilities are typically repurposed unused oil wells, salt mines, or aquifers.
Depleted gas reservoirs (underground caverns that once held natural gas, reused by pumping gas back in) are the most common storage type; salt caverns and aquifers are the other common types.
Precise valuation of a storage facility requires a path-dependent option calculation; because this is complex, approximations such as intrinsic value are commonly used in practice instead.

Aquifers are water reservoirs repurposed to store natural gas; they are the least desirable and most expensive storage type, built only where they offer a strong geographic advantage over other options (i.e., the only viable option in that location).
Aquifers have the lowest working-gas-to-total-volume ratio and the slowest injection/withdrawal cycle of any storage facility type.

Because no gas exists in an aquifer at construction, a large volume must be injected before operation, and unlike other storage types there is little room to draw down the cushion gas without impairing the facility's ability to function.

A worked auction-bid valuation example combines a seasonal trade (buy in low-price spring and fall, sell in higher-price summer and winter) with a weekday/weekend trade (buy weekend, sell weekday, using the two weekend days for injection).
Most facilities can only do one full seasonal cycle a year; the example facility in the trading exercise is high-performance and can cycle twice.

Running the weekday/weekend trade alongside the seasonal trade leaves only 3 net days per week for the seasonal trade's injection/delivery instead of 7, since the two trades compete for the same physical injection/withdrawal capacity.
Valuing an auction bid requires optimizing across possible trade combinations to find the most profitable feasible mix.
The EIA publishes a weekly report on the amount of natural gas in storage, consisting of a table of regional storage volumes and a chart comparing current total storage to the prior five years.
relationships: Serves as the buffer implied by pipeline pressure dynamics.
Facility geology determines base gas requirements and withdrawal speed.
Connects storage economics to option pricing concepts used elsewhere in the text.
Contrasts with salt cavern storage as a much lower-performance, higher-cost storage type (aquifers).
The auction-bid arbitrage example draws directly on the Cycling, Deliverability, and Injection Capacity definitions.
The EIA weekly report provides the public data traders would use when valuing storage capacity, as in the Natural Gas Storage Arbitrage Bid Strategy example.
trading_implications: Traders and analysts often rely on intrinsic value as a practical approximation rather than solving the full path-dependent option problem when valuing a storage facility.
Aquifer storage capacity is poorly suited to fast-cycling or short-term arbitrage strategies given its slow deliverability.

Valuing storage capacity for an auction bid requires optimizing across a seasonal trade and a weekday/weekend trade, which compete for the same physical injection/withdrawal capacity, so operational limits may make it infeasible to run both simultaneously year-round.
caveats: Most facilities can only do one full cycle a year; the trading example's facility is high-performance and can cycle twice, so its economics are not representative of a typical facility.
Exact storage valuation is a path-dependent option calculation; intrinsic value is a commonly used approximation, not the precise value.
Aquifer storage cushion gas cannot be drawn down significantly without impairing the facility's ability to function, unlike other storage types.
